newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rises may be "too little too late" for stg.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rises may be "too little too late" for stg.

text.p: The apparent reticence to raise interest rates before the election is raising concern in the foreign exchange market that the British authorities might be getting behind in their quest to keep inflation low, analysts said on Friday.

Even though interest rates are widely expected to rise after the election, it might be too late for the pound to benefit from tightening as the market might view an increase at this point as "too little, too late".

Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke has based his steady-rates argument on a recent spate of soft economic data and the deflationary impact of the strong pound. But growth is likely to remain above trend, maintaining the case for higher rates, economists said.

Expectations that British rates still have room to rise have fuelled the pound's meteoric rise. But since soft data have put those hopes on a backburner, the pound has shed ground, losing about ten pfennigs in two weeks. Around 1400 gmt it stood at 2.6252 marks and $1.6022.
The received wisdom is that sterling will recover some lost ground on the back of post-election rate rises.
"It might not be as simple as that," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.
"Once the market thinks Clarke is behind the game, the game is up -- even if rates are increased -- because the market thinks it's "too little too late'," he said.

The debate about the impact of the strong pound on the economy has become increasingly polarised. BOE Governor George last week gave a forthright warning of the inflationary danger of allowing a strong currency to delay a rate rise.
Despite recent soft data growth is expected to remain above trend, which implies a pick-up in inflation and underscores the case for higher rates, economists said.
However, the Confederation of British Industry said sterling's performance subdued cost pressures in the manufacturing and export sectors.

British exporters, meanwhile, have warned that pound strength is reducing their earnings. A strong currency reduces export demand as it makes a country's products more expensive abroad, and encourages imports.
Analysts said Clarke's thought pattern that a strong pound is reason to keep rates steady might eventually backfire on the currency.

"The Chancellor says you don't have to raise rates because sterling is so strong, but sterling is so strong because rates are (perceived to be) going up," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel in London.
Traders are worried that political considerations rather than economic prudency are behind Clarke's decision to hold rates.
With the election looming by May at the lastest, an electorate already disenchanted with the ruling Conservatives might not take another tightening lightly, analysts said.
Further support for Clarke's steady-rates stance came on Friday from British Treasury adviser Martin Weale, who said there is no immediate need for a rise in rates.
But if the pound falls significantly, policy will have to be tightened, said Weale, who is also head of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR), a leading think-tank.

Weale expects sterling's strength to knock almost a full percentage point off British growth in 1997. Hence the NIESR cut its GDP forecast for next year to 2.5 percent growth from 3.5 percent estimated previously.
Export growth would halve in 1997 to 3.5 percent, the NIESR predicted in its quarterly review.
But the risk that inflation will pick up is more likely to come from consumer demand, which is only marginally influenced by the pound's gyrations, economists said.
"Consumer demand is likely to remain the driving force of UK growth and the key to the above trend economic activity," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi in London.
